Level 1: Computer

Computer

A desktop computer: the system unit (tower), shown with its side panel removed, and the input and output devices connected to it.

What is it?

A computer is a machine that stores and processes information by following instructions called programs. The desktop tower (the “system unit”) holds the parts that do the work. Around it are input devices, such as the keyboard, mouse, joystick and webcam, and output devices, such as the monitor, speakers and printer.

What does it do?

It takes input (keystrokes, clicks, network data), processes it in the CPU and GPU, keeps working data in RAM, saves files to storage, and sends results to outputs such as the screen and speakers.

Why it matters

Every part has one job, and the whole system is only as fast as its slowest link. Knowing what each part does helps you choose upgrades, fix problems and understand how software really runs.

Real-life examples

  • Gaming desktopFast GPU, 6–8+ core CPU, 32 GB RAM
  • Office PCIntegrated graphics, 16 GB RAM
  • WorkstationMany CPU cores, 64–256 GB RAM
  • Mini PCLaptop-class parts in a small box

Key specifications

Form factor
ATX mid-tower (shown)
Main parts
CPU, motherboard, RAM, GPU, storage, PSU, cooling, I/O
Power draw
about 60–600 W depending on load

Fun fact

The CPU in this tower contains tens of billions of transistors. ENIAC, a famous computer from 1945, used about 17,500 vacuum tubes and filled a large room.
